Proposition 2: Rainy Day Fund
Proposition 2: Rainy Day Fund
Proposition 2: Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment
Additional Titles
Budget Stabilization Account Cap Increase and Gann Limit Changes Amendment
Rainy day Fund
Raise limit on rainy day fund deposits
Summary
Proposition 2 was placed on the ballot by the California Legislature as Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email) The amendment was introduced on June 25, 2026 and it passed the state Assembly by a vote of 59-8, with 12 not voting. It passed the state Senate by a vote of 29-2, with nine not voting.
Proposition 2 on the November 2026 ballot would amend the State Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codesTOCSelected.xhtml?tocCode=CONS&tocTitle=+California+Constitution+-+CONS) by changing California’s rainy day fund rules to build larger reserves and better protect public services during economic downturns and other budget emergencies. Specifically, it would require the state to make deposits into the fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of the current 10 percent of General Fund taxes).
It would also expand the types of state debt that can be repaid with General Fund money set aside each year and require the extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of the current date of 2030). In addition, Prop. 2 would change how certain reserves are treated under the state spending cap, or “Gann Limit (https://www.cde.ca.gov/fg/ac/gl/),” making it easier to save more money when revenues are strong. The Legislature placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot through Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20).
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 2 would allow California to build a larger financial cushion by raising the maximum size of the state’s rainy day fund. It would also direct a greater share of unusually strong revenues into savings during high-revenue years. Having more money set aside could give the state greater flexibility during economic downturns or other periods when tax collections fall short of expectations.
Proposition 2 would extend requirements for additional state debt payments through 2040. As a result, California could pay down more of its outstanding debts and long-term financial obligations than it otherwise would under current rules.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports changing California’s rainy day fund rules to allow larger reserves, increase deposits when revenues are strong, extend required debt payments through 2040, and change how certain reserves are treated under the state spending limit. It would also allow the governor’s May budget revision to serve as a declaration of a budget emergency when certain conditions are met.
NO: A “no” vote opposes these changes and would keep the current rules for the state’s rainy day fund, extra debt payments, spending limit, and declarations of budget emergencies.

Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional

ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
The State Budget
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion
from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. The General Fund is the account the
state uses to pay for most public services. About half of this spending is for schools, community
colleges, and the state’s public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending
level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for
health and human services programs, mainly for the state’s low-income health insurance
program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
How Does the State Raise Revenue? The income tax is the state’s largest tax. It pays for
most spending from the General Fund. Other major taxes include the corporation tax and the
sales tax. Much of the income tax is paid by high-income taxpayers, whose incomes often
include gains from stocks and other investments.
State Revenues Are Unpredictable. State revenues go up and down a lot from year to year.
This is because revenues depend on how the economy and stock market are doing. When things
are going well, revenues can grow quickly. When things are going badly, like during a recession
or a stock market crash, revenues can decline by tens of billions of dollars. During a bad
recession or market crash, total revenue declines over a few years can equal 50 percent or more
of annual General Fund revenues.
The State Must Meet Certain Budgeting Requirements Each Year. The State Constitution
requires the Legislature to pass a balanced budget each year. This means the state cannot adopt a
budget that spends more money than is available. In addition, the State Constitution limits how
much tax revenue the state can spend. This limit is called the “state appropriations limit.” Certain
kinds of spending—like infrastructure—do not count toward the limit. All other spending,
including money put into reserves, does count toward the limit.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 2 of 4
Reserves
Reserves Allow the State to Maintain Spending When Revenues Decline. The state puts
money into reserves when the economy is doing well. This means that money is saved instead of
being spent on public programs during these periods of time. When the economy gets worse and
revenues decline, the state uses reserves to help maintain spending on public programs. Reserves
help the state avoid some spending cuts, tax increases, and borrowing to balance the budget.
Currently, the state has about $20 billion in reserves that can be used for any public program.
State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the “Rainy Day Fund.” The State
Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state’s
main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year. Money in the
rainy day fund can be used for any state program. In addition, the state must put more money
into the rainy day fund in years when revenue from taxes on investment gains is higher than
normal. During a budget emergency, the state can stop making deposits and/or take money out of
the rainy day fund.
Savings Are No Longer Required Once the Rainy Day Fund Reaches a Certain Level.
Once money in the rainy day fund reaches 10 percent of General Fund taxes, the state is no
longer required to make additional deposits. The money that would have gone into the rainy day
fund instead must be spent on infrastructure (like highways and housing).
Debt
The State Has Different Kinds of Debts. The state has more than $250 billion in debts. These
include debt for infrastructure and pension and retiree health benefits earned by state employees.
The state also sometimes borrows money from other state funds to help pay General Fund costs.
State debts are repaid over time, usually according to a schedule or plan. Each year, the state
makes payments toward its debts.
State Constitution Requires the State to Make Extra Debt Payments Toward Pension and
Health Benefits. The State Constitution requires the state to make extra debt payments above
those normally made each year. The amount of these extra debt payments is the same as the
amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. The state may only use these extra
debt payments to pay down long-term pension and retiree health care debts. Making extra
payments toward these debts saves the state money in the long run.
Extra Debt Payments Optional After 2030. The requirement for extra debt payments ends in
2030. After that, the Legislature and the Governor could decide to deposit the money for extra
debt payments into the rainy day fund instead. Or, the Legislature and the Governor could make
smaller extra debt payments and put the rest of the money into the rainy day fund.

Page 3 of 4
PROPOSAL
Save More in the Rainy Day Fund. Proposition 2 requires the state to make deposits into the
rainy day fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of 10 percent of General
Fund taxes). In addition, the state would make even larger deposits in years when revenues from
taxes on investment gains are very high, like when the stock market is booming.
Extend and Expand Extra Debt Payments. Proposition 2 also requires the state to make
extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of through 2030). These debt payments would be the
same as the amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. In addition, the amount
set aside for extra debt payments could be used for an expanded set of purposes. Specifically,
these payments could be used to make required payments to schools and community colleges,
repay borrowing from other state funds, and repay certain loans from the federal government.
Change How Rainy Day Fund Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit.
Deposits into the rainy day fund would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead,
the money would count toward the limit when it is taken out.
Change How Other Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit. The state has
an account to set aside funds when revenues are surging. By setting these funds aside, the state
can avoid overspending when revenue estimates are particularly uncertain. Under Proposition 2,
deposits into this account also would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead, the
money would count toward the limit when it is taken out. This exclusion could not be larger than
10 percent of General Fund taxes in each year.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Budget Reserves Would Be Higher. By continuing to require deposits into the rainy day fund
until the balance reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes, the state would save more over time.
In addition, by depositing more money when revenues are surging, the state likely would save
more in the rainy day fund in certain years. More reserves would make balancing the budget
somewhat easier when revenues decline.
Possibly More Debt Payments. By requiring the state to make extra debt payments through
2040, the state might make more debt payments than it would without Proposition 2.

YES/NO STATEMENT
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying
down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The
state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
A NO vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down
extra state debts would not change.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT
• State budget reserves would be higher.
BALLOT LABEL
Fiscal Impact: State budget reserves would be higher.

November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 1 of 4
PROPOSITION 2
Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional
Amendment.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
The State Budget
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion
from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. The General Fund is the account the
state uses to pay for most public services. About half of this spending is for schools, community
colleges, and the state’s public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending
level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for
health and human services programs, mainly for the state’s low-income health insurance
program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
How Does the State Raise Revenue? The income tax is the state’s largest tax. It pays for
most spending from the General Fund. Other major taxes include the corporation tax and the
sales tax. Much of the income tax is paid by high-income taxpayers, whose incomes often
include gains from stocks and other investments.
State Revenues Are Unpredictable. State revenues go up and down a lot from year to year.
This is because revenues depend on how the economy and stock market are doing. When things
are going well, revenues can grow quickly. When things are going badly, like during a recession
or a stock market crash, revenues can decline by tens of billions of dollars. During a bad
recession or market crash, total revenue declines over a few years can equal 50 percent or more
of annual General Fund revenues.
The State Must Meet Certain Budgeting Requirements Each Year. The State Constitution
requires the Legislature to pass a balanced budget each year. This means the state cannot adopt a
budget that spends more money than is available. In addition, the State Constitution limits how
much tax revenue the state can spend. This limit is called the “state appropriations limit.” Certain
kinds of spending—like infrastructure—do not count toward the limit. All other spending,
including money put into reserves, does count toward the limit.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 2 of 4
Reserves
Reserves Allow the State to Maintain Spending When Revenues Decline. The state puts
money into reserves when the economy is doing well. This means that money is saved instead of
being spent on public programs during these periods of time. When the economy gets worse and
revenues decline, the state uses reserves to help maintain spending on public programs. Reserves
help the state avoid some spending cuts, tax increases, and borrowing to balance the budget.
Currently, the state has about $20 billion in reserves that can be used for any public program.
State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the “Rainy Day Fund.” The State
Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state’s
main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year. Money in the
rainy day fund can be used for any state program. In addition, the state must put more money
into the rainy day fund in years when revenue from taxes on investment gains is higher than
normal. During a budget emergency, the state can stop making deposits and/or take money out of
the rainy day fund.
Savings Are No Longer Required Once the Rainy Day Fund Reaches a Certain Level.
Once money in the rainy day fund reaches 10 percent of General Fund taxes, the state is no
longer required to make additional deposits. The money that would have gone into the rainy day
fund instead must be spent on infrastructure (like highways and housing).
Debt
The State Has Different Kinds of Debts. The state has more than $250 billion in debts. These
include debt for infrastructure and pension and retiree health benefits earned by state employees.
The state also sometimes borrows money from other state funds to help pay General Fund costs.
State debts are repaid over time, usually according to a schedule or plan. Each year, the state
makes payments toward its debts.
State Constitution Requires the State to Make Extra Debt Payments Toward Pension and
Health Benefits. The State Constitution requires the state to make extra debt payments above
those normally made each year. The amount of these extra debt payments is the same as the
amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. The state may only use these extra
debt payments to pay down long-term pension and retiree health care debts. Making extra
payments toward these debts saves the state money in the long run.
Extra Debt Payments Optional After 2030. The requirement for extra debt payments ends in
2030. After that, the Legislature and the Governor could decide to deposit the money for extra
debt payments into the rainy day fund instead. Or, the Legislature and the Governor could make
smaller extra debt payments and put the rest of the money into the rainy day fund.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 3 of 4
PROPOSAL
Save More in the Rainy Day Fund. Proposition 2 requires the state to make deposits into the
rainy day fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of 10 percent of General
Fund taxes). In addition, the state would make even larger deposits in years when revenues from
taxes on investment gains are very high, like when the stock market is booming.
Extend and Expand Extra Debt Payments. Proposition 2 also requires the state to make
extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of through 2030). These debt payments would be the
same as the amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. In addition, the amount
set aside for extra debt payments could be used for an expanded set of purposes. Specifically,
these payments could be used to make required payments to schools and community colleges,
repay borrowing from other state funds, and repay certain loans from the federal government.
Change How Rainy Day Fund Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit.
Deposits into the rainy day fund would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead,
the money would count toward the limit when it is taken out.
Change How Other Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit. The state has
an account to set aside funds when revenues are surging. By setting these funds aside, the state
can avoid overspending when revenue estimates are particularly uncertain. Under Proposition 2,
deposits into this account also would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead, the
money would count toward the limit when it is taken out. This exclusion could not be larger than
10 percent of General Fund taxes in each year.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Budget Reserves Would Be Higher. By continuing to require deposits into the rainy day fund
until the balance reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes, the state would save more over time.
In addition, by depositing more money when revenues are surging, the state likely would save
more in the rainy day fund in certain years. More reserves would make balancing the budget
somewhat easier when revenues decline.
Possibly More Debt Payments. By requiring the state to make extra debt payments through
2040, the state might make more debt payments than it would without Proposition 2.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 4 of 4
YES/NO STATEMENT
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying
down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The
state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
A NO vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down
extra state debts would not change.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT
• State budget reserves would be higher.
BALLOT LABEL
Fiscal Impact: State budget reserves would be higher.

Proposition 2: Rainy Day Fund
Proposition 2: Rainy Day Fund
Proposition 2: Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment
Additional Titles
Budget Stabilization Account Cap Increase and Gann Limit Changes Amendment
Rainy day Fund
Raise limit on rainy day fund deposits
Summary
Proposition 2 was placed on the ballot by the California Legislature as Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email) The amendment was introduced on June 25, 2026 and it passed the state Assembly by a vote of 59-8, with 12 not voting. It passed the state Senate by a vote of 29-2, with nine not voting.
Proposition 2 on the November 2026 ballot would amend the State Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codesTOCSelected.xhtml?tocCode=CONS&tocTitle=+California+Constitution+-+CONS) by changing California’s rainy day fund rules to build larger reserves and better protect public services during economic downturns and other budget emergencies. Specifically, it would require the state to make deposits into the fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of the current 10 percent of General Fund taxes).
It would also expand the types of state debt that can be repaid with General Fund money set aside each year and require the extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of the current date of 2030). In addition, Prop. 2 would change how certain reserves are treated under the state spending cap, or “Gann Limit (https://www.cde.ca.gov/fg/ac/gl/),” making it easier to save more money when revenues are strong. The Legislature placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot through Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20).
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 2 would allow California to build a larger financial cushion by raising the maximum size of the state’s rainy day fund. It would also direct a greater share of unusually strong revenues into savings during high-revenue years. Having more money set aside could give the state greater flexibility during economic downturns or other periods when tax collections fall short of expectations.
Proposition 2 would extend requirements for additional state debt payments through 2040. As a result, California could pay down more of its outstanding debts and long-term financial obligations than it otherwise would under current rules.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports changing California’s rainy day fund rules to allow larger reserves, increase deposits when revenues are strong, extend required debt payments through 2040, and change how certain reserves are treated under the state spending limit. It would also allow the governor’s May budget revision to serve as a declaration of a budget emergency when certain conditions are met.
NO: A “no” vote opposes these changes and would keep the current rules for the state’s rainy day fund, extra debt payments, spending limit, and declarations of budget emergencies.

November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 1 of 4
PROPOSITION 2
Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional
Amendment.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
The State Budget
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion
from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. The General Fund is the account the
state uses to pay for most public services. About half of this spending is for schools, community
colleges, and the state’s public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending
level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for
health and human services programs, mainly for the state’s low-income health insurance
program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
How Does the State Raise Revenue? The income tax is the state’s largest tax. It pays for
most spending from the General Fund. Other major taxes include the corporation tax and the
sales tax. Much of the income tax is paid by high-income taxpayers, whose incomes often
include gains from stocks and other investments.
State Revenues Are Unpredictable. State revenues go up and down a lot from year to year.
This is because revenues depend on how the economy and stock market are doing. When things
are going well, revenues can grow quickly. When things are going badly, like during a recession
or a stock market crash, revenues can decline by tens of billions of dollars. During a bad
recession or market crash, total revenue declines over a few years can equal 50 percent or more
of annual General Fund revenues.
The State Must Meet Certain Budgeting Requirements Each Year. The State Constitution
requires the Legislature to pass a balanced budget each year. This means the state cannot adopt a
budget that spends more money than is available. In addition, the State Constitution limits how
much tax revenue the state can spend. This limit is called the “state appropriations limit.” Certain
kinds of spending—like infrastructure—do not count toward the limit. All other spending,
including money put into reserves, does count toward the limit.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 2 of 4
Reserves
Reserves Allow the State to Maintain Spending When Revenues Decline. The state puts
money into reserves when the economy is doing well. This means that money is saved instead of
being spent on public programs during these periods of time. When the economy gets worse and
revenues decline, the state uses reserves to help maintain spending on public programs. Reserves
help the state avoid some spending cuts, tax increases, and borrowing to balance the budget.
Currently, the state has about $20 billion in reserves that can be used for any public program.
State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the “Rainy Day Fund.” The State
Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state’s
main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year. Money in the
rainy day fund can be used for any state program. In addition, the state must put more money
into the rainy day fund in years when revenue from taxes on investment gains is higher than
normal. During a budget emergency, the state can stop making deposits and/or take money out of
the rainy day fund.
Savings Are No Longer Required Once the Rainy Day Fund Reaches a Certain Level.
Once money in the rainy day fund reaches 10 percent of General Fund taxes, the state is no
longer required to make additional deposits. The money that would have gone into the rainy day
fund instead must be spent on infrastructure (like highways and housing).
Debt
The State Has Different Kinds of Debts. The state has more than $250 billion in debts. These
include debt for infrastructure and pension and retiree health benefits earned by state employees.
The state also sometimes borrows money from other state funds to help pay General Fund costs.
State debts are repaid over time, usually according to a schedule or plan. Each year, the state
makes payments toward its debts.
State Constitution Requires the State to Make Extra Debt Payments Toward Pension and
Health Benefits. The State Constitution requires the state to make extra debt payments above
those normally made each year. The amount of these extra debt payments is the same as the
amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. The state may only use these extra
debt payments to pay down long-term pension and retiree health care debts. Making extra
payments toward these debts saves the state money in the long run.
Extra Debt Payments Optional After 2030. The requirement for extra debt payments ends in
2030. After that, the Legislature and the Governor could decide to deposit the money for extra
debt payments into the rainy day fund instead. Or, the Legislature and the Governor could make
smaller extra debt payments and put the rest of the money into the rainy day fund.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 3 of 4
PROPOSAL
Save More in the Rainy Day Fund. Proposition 2 requires the state to make deposits into the
rainy day fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of 10 percent of General
Fund taxes). In addition, the state would make even larger deposits in years when revenues from
taxes on investment gains are very high, like when the stock market is booming.
Extend and Expand Extra Debt Payments. Proposition 2 also requires the state to make
extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of through 2030). These debt payments would be the
same as the amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. In addition, the amount
set aside for extra debt payments could be used for an expanded set of purposes. Specifically,
these payments could be used to make required payments to schools and community colleges,
repay borrowing from other state funds, and repay certain loans from the federal government.
Change How Rainy Day Fund Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit.
Deposits into the rainy day fund would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead,
the money would count toward the limit when it is taken out.
Change How Other Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit. The state has
an account to set aside funds when revenues are surging. By setting these funds aside, the state
can avoid overspending when revenue estimates are particularly uncertain. Under Proposition 2,
deposits into this account also would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead, the
money would count toward the limit when it is taken out. This exclusion could not be larger than
10 percent of General Fund taxes in each year.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Budget Reserves Would Be Higher. By continuing to require deposits into the rainy day fund
until the balance reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes, the state would save more over time.
In addition, by depositing more money when revenues are surging, the state likely would save
more in the rainy day fund in certain years. More reserves would make balancing the budget
somewhat easier when revenues decline.
Possibly More Debt Payments. By requiring the state to make extra debt payments through
2040, the state might make more debt payments than it would without Proposition 2.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 4 of 4
YES/NO STATEMENT
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying
down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The
state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
A NO vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down
extra state debts would not change.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT
• State budget reserves would be higher.
BALLOT LABEL
Fiscal Impact: State budget reserves would be higher.

Raise limit on rainy day fund deposits
This constitutional amendment would allow the state to deposit up to 20% of its general fund tax revenue in the state’s reserves, up from the current ceiling of 10%. The deposits would not count toward the voter-approved Gann Limit, which caps the amount state lawmakers can spend each year and requires excess funds to be returned to the people. It also authorizes spending some tax revenue to pay down California’s $20 billion federal unemployment insurance debt. The California Legislature placed this measure on the ballot.

# Proposition 2 — Doubles the State’s “Rainy Day Fund” and Lets Sacramento Sidestep Constitutional Spending Limits
*Increases the slush fund that Sacramento uses to finance such exotic programs as healthcare for illegal immigrants.*
Proposition 2 would raise the cap on the state’s Budget Stabilization Account — commonly called the rainy day fund — from 10% to 20% of General Fund tax revenue.
It would also exclude deposits into that account from the state’s constitutional spending limit (known as the Gann Limit, which voters established through Proposition 4 in 1979).
This means that, if Proposition 2 is approved by voters, the state will have a larger rainy day fund, and that the Gann limit would not apply to spending from that account.
**Supporters** argue that a larger reserve helps the state absorb the swings in revenue that come from relying heavily on income and capital-gains taxes paid by high earners.
Supporters include Governor Gavin Newsom and the California Democratic Party.
**Opponents** argue that the enactment of the Gann Limit was designed specifically to force the government to return excess revenue to taxpayers or schools rather than retain it, and that exempting rainy day deposits from that calculation loosens one of the state’s few constraints on the growth of government spending.
Opponents include the California Republican Party, State Assemblyman Joe Patterson and Reform California.

## What is the Gann Limit?
Passed in 1979, the Gann Limit (aka State Appropriations Limit, SAL, or Proposition 4) capped per capita tax revenue spending at 1979 levels and required the excess be distributed to tax payers in a rebate.
In 1988, voters amended the constitutional regulations to be adjusted for inflation, calculated over a two-year period, and significantly changed how the excess money could be distributed (outlined in the bullets below).
It’s not often that the Gann Limit is exceeded, however this is the second year in a row the budget will be operating within these boundaries — highlighting the deep, growing income inequality in the state.

Proposition 2
Raise limit on rainy day fund deposits
This constitutional amendment would allow the state to deposit up to 20% of its general fund tax revenue in the state’s reserves, up from the current ceiling of 10%. The deposits would not count toward the voter-approved Gann Limit, which caps the amount state lawmakers can spend each year and requires excess funds to be returned to the people. It also authorizes spending some tax revenue to pay down California’s $20 billion federal unemployment insurance debt. The California Legislature placed this measure on the ballot.

Proposition 2
Raise limit on rainy day fund deposits
This constitutional amendment would allow the state to deposit up to 20% of its general fund tax revenue in the state’s reserves, up from the current ceiling of 10%. The deposits would not count toward the voter-approved Gann Limit, which caps the amount state lawmakers can spend each year and requires excess funds to be returned to the people. It also authorizes spending some tax revenue to pay down California’s $20 billion federal unemployment insurance debt. The California Legislature placed this measure on the ballot.

# Proposition 2 — Doubles the State’s “Rainy Day Fund” and Lets Sacramento Sidestep Constitutional Spending Limits
*Increases the slush fund that Sacramento uses to finance such exotic programs as healthcare for illegal immigrants.*
Proposition 2 would raise the cap on the state’s Budget Stabilization Account — commonly called the rainy day fund — from 10% to 20% of General Fund tax revenue.
It would also exclude deposits into that account from the state’s constitutional spending limit (known as the Gann Limit, which voters established through Proposition 4 in 1979).
This means that, if Proposition 2 is approved by voters, the state will have a larger rainy day fund, and that the Gann limit would not apply to spending from that account.
**Supporters** argue that a larger reserve helps the state absorb the swings in revenue that come from relying heavily on income and capital-gains taxes paid by high earners.
Supporters include Governor Gavin Newsom and the California Democratic Party.
**Opponents** argue that the enactment of the Gann Limit was designed specifically to force the government to return excess revenue to taxpayers or schools rather than retain it, and that exempting rainy day deposits from that calculation loosens one of the state’s few constraints on the growth of government spending.
Opponents include the California Republican Party, State Assemblyman Joe Patterson and Reform California.
**CPC’s Take: NO

**This Proposition:** Proposition 2 (2026), "Save for California's Future Act" (ACA 20), a legislative constitutional amendment. Passed by the Assembly 59-8 and by the Senate 29-2.

**Contents:**
1. Raise the BSA (rainy day fund) cap from 10% → 20% of General Fund tax revenue.
2. Larger mandatory deposits in years when capital gains tax revenue surges.
3. Extend mandatory additional debt repayment (pension/retiree health care, now also school minimum funding, budget borrowing, federal UI loan of about $20 billion) from 2030 → 2040.
4. Change in Gann Limit treatment: deposits into BSA and PSHF (up to 10% of GF taxes per year) don't count against the state appropriations limit; withdrawals count against it.

**Support:**
- LAO (nonpartisan): Has long recommended significantly larger reserves (per IJPR, LAO's April 2025 report said the state should be saved gradually up to 50% of General Fund taxes); the LAO's August 2024 handout emphasizes that BSA max (10%) is "in stark contrast" to recession-scale revenue declines (~50% of GF taxes); current reserve (~$17-20 billion) is "significantly exceeded" by typical recession-scale budget problems.
- SPUR (nonpartisan urban policy): supports.
- IGS (UC Berkeley): neutral guide, notes broad support.
- Sacramento Bee (editorial board): supports. SF Chronicle: supports.
- Newsom, Democratic legislative conference, LA Chamber of Commerce, California Professional Firefighters, hospital/primary care associations, State Board of Education president, former HHS Secretary Becerra.
- Fiscal logic: California revenue is extremely volatile (stock-market dependent); 2022-23 had a $100 billion surplus, then 2024-25 and 2025-26 had roughly $50 billion deficits (Medi-Cal federal funding cuts). A larger reserve is a buffer that prevents mid-year cuts to schools/Medi-Cal/public safety.
- Debt repayment extension: saves interest on pension/retiree health care liabilities and pays down the $20 billion federal UI loan — a net long-term savings.
- The Gann Limit accounting change is economically neutral in the long run (money counts when spent, not when saved); and importantly, under current rules, saving money ratchets up the spending cap (deposits count against the cap, and the cap is based on the prior year's appropriations). The proposed rule stops that ratchet effect on savings.

**Opposition:**
- Taxpayer rebate avoidance (the main argument). But factual background: The Gann Limit rebate has only been triggered three times in California history: FY 1987-88 ($1.1 billion), FY 2020-21 ($2.8 billion GSS I), FY 2021-22 ($6 billion GSS II). In 2022-23, despite a $100+ billion surplus, no rebate was needed (and in any case, the state saved $104 billion in reserves). Opponents' "cancels your tax rebate" argument is mostly theoretical; in the current political reality, the state's surpluses have been directed to spending/reserves.
- "Slush fund" / spending limit erosion argument (Reform California/DeMaio, California Policy Center, Assemblymember Tangipa, legislative Republicans). CPC: "Saving money always sounds great until you learn what..." (cut off) — an ideological anti-spending-limit stance.
- The measure does not "create new funding" for schools or health care — true, it's a macro-fiscal stability measure; the "protects schools" claim is about avoiding future cuts, not new money.

**Considerations:**
- 20% cap (about $170-200 billion) is still below the LAO's recommended ~50% and below the scale of a severe recession (50% of annual revenue).
- Withdrawal guardrails remain: the Governor's budget emergency declaration + legislative vote; withdrawals are limited to the amount needed to maintain spending at the highest of the past three enacted budgets, or half the BSA balance.
- Timing: 2026 revenue is coming in strong (KPBS: AI-driven revenue surge), and the state just emerged from a $50 billion deficit — exactly when proponents argue saving is most important.

**Media endorsement split:** Sacramento Bee and SF Chronicle for; San Diego Union-Tribune and Orange County Register against (the OC Register's headline "fiscal discipline, not accounting tricks" frames this as an accounting trick).

Weighing all this: the nonpartisan fiscal expert community (LAO) explicitly supports building larger reserves; the measure's fiscal impact is moderate and well-guarded; the core opponent argument (rebate) rests on a mechanism that has only been triggered 3 times in 47 years (and 2 of those were pandemic stimulus payments that the state chose to satisfy in that form); the measure also mandates long-term interest savings via debt repayment. The "slush fund" concern is mitigated by the existing withdrawal rules and the fact that the Gann Limit accounting change is roughly neutral long-term (and even removes the current ratchet problem where saving permanently raises the spending cap).

One more thing to verify: the LAO's recommendation of 50% — IJPR article from April 2025: "The LAO released a report saying Newsom should push it to 50%, but do it gradually." This is from Newsom's 2025-26 budget proposal (raising the cap to 20%, excluding deposits from the Gann Limit) — and the LAO said he should go further. This strongly supports the "yes" position.

Also, the KPBS article is worth checking to understand the current (October 2026) context. And I could also read the full CBP Center brief, which appears to be in favor. But I think I have enough information. Let me quickly grab the KPBS article to check the current fiscal context and see if there's anything surprising (e.g., an argument that since revenue is currently strong, the state should be saving — supporting "yes"; or an opposing argument that the surplus should be returned).

Actually, let me also quickly confirm that the current state of the state's reserves is as described (the state just spent a lot of its reserve on the 2024-25 and 2025-26 deficits). The LAO's analysis says "currently, the state has about $20 billion in usable reserves for any public program." That's consistent.

I'm confident: **yes**.

Let me quickly grab the KPBS article to confirm the current context, then answer.
I have a strong evidence base now. Let me do one final check on the current fiscal context (2026 revenue environment) to confirm the timing argument.

Now I've got a really rich overall picture. Let me organize everything:

**This Proposition:** Proposition 2 (2026), "Save for California's Future Act" (ACA 20), a legislative constitutional amendment. Passed by the Assembly 59-8 and by the Senate 29-2.

**Contents:**
1. Raise the BSA (rainy day fund) cap from 10% → 20% of General Fund tax revenue.
2. Larger mandatory deposits in years when capital gains tax revenue surges.
3. Extend mandatory additional debt repayment (pension/retiree health care, now also school minimum funding, budget borrowing, federal UI loan of about $20 billion) from 2030 → 2040.
4. Change in Gann Limit treatment: deposits into BSA and PSHF (up to 10% of GF taxes per year) don't count against the state appropriations limit; withdrawals count against it.

**Support:**
- LAO (nonpartisan): Has long recommended significantly larger reserves (per IJPR, LAO's April 2025 report said the state should be saved gradually up to 50% of General Fund taxes); the LAO's August 2024 handout emphasizes that BSA max (10%) is "in stark contrast" to recession-scale revenue declines (~50% of GF taxes); current reserve (~$17-20 billion) is "significantly exceeded" by typical recession-scale budget problems.
- SPUR (nonpartisan urban policy): supports.
- IGS (UC Berkeley): neutral guide, notes broad support.
- Sacramento Bee (editorial board): supports. SF Chronicle: supports.
- Newsom, Democratic legislative conference, LA Chamber of Commerce, California Professional Firefighters, hospital/primary care associations, State Board of Education president, former HHS Secretary Becerra.
- Fiscal logic: California revenue is extremely volatile (stock-market dependent); 2022-23 had a $100 billion surplus, then 2024-25 and 2025-26 had roughly $50 billion deficits (Medi-Cal federal funding cuts). A larger reserve is a buffer that prevents mid-year cuts to schools/Medi-Cal/public safety.
- Debt repayment extension: saves interest on pension/retiree health care liabilities and pays down the $20 billion federal UI loan — a net long-term savings.
- The Gann Limit accounting change is economically neutral in the long run (money counts when spent, not when saved); and importantly, under current rules, saving money ratchets up the spending cap (deposits count against the cap, and the cap is based on the prior year's appropriations). The proposed rule stops that ratchet effect on savings.

**Opposition:**
- Taxpayer rebate avoidance (the main argument). But factual background: The Gann Limit rebate has only been triggered three times in California history: FY 1987-88 ($1.1 billion), FY 2020-21 ($2.8 billion GSS I), FY 2021-22 ($6 billion GSS II). In 2022-23, despite a $100+ billion surplus, no rebate was needed (and in any case, the state saved $104 billion in reserves). Opponents' "cancels your tax rebate" argument is mostly theoretical; in the current political reality, the state's surpluses have been directed to spending/reserves.
- "Slush fund" / spending limit erosion argument (Reform California/DeMaio, California Policy Center, Assemblymember Tangipa, legislative Republicans). CPC: "Saving money always sounds great until you learn what..." (cut off) — an ideological anti-spending-limit stance.
- The measure does not "create new funding" for schools or health care — true, it's a macro-fiscal stability measure; the "protects schools" claim is about avoiding future cuts, not new money.

**Considerations:**
- 20% cap (about $170-200 billion) is still below the LAO's recommended ~50% and below the scale of a severe recession (50% of annual revenue).
- Withdrawal guardrails remain: the Governor's budget emergency declaration + legislative vote; withdrawals are limited to the amount needed to maintain spending at the highest of the past three enacted budgets, or half the BSA balance.
- Timing: 2026 revenue is coming in strong (KPBS: AI-driven revenue surge), and the state just emerged from a $50 billion deficit — exactly when proponents argue saving is most important.

**Media endorsement split:** Sacramento Bee and SF Chronicle for; San Diego Union-Tribune and Orange County Register against (the OC Register's headline "fiscal discipline, not accounting tricks" frames this as an accounting trick).

Weighing all this: the nonpartisan fiscal expert community (LAO) explicitly supports building larger reserves; the measure's fiscal impact is moderate and well-guarded; the core opponent argument (rebate) rests on a mechanism that has only been triggered 3 times in 47 years (and 2 of those were pandemic stimulus payments that the state chose to satisfy in that form); the measure also mandates long-term interest savings via debt repayment. The "slush fund" concern is mitigated by the existing withdrawal rules and the fact that the Gann Limit accounting change is roughly neutral long-term (and even removes the current ratchet problem where saving permanently raises the spending cap).

One more thing to verify: the LAO's recommendation of 50% — IJPR article from April 2025: "The LAO released a report saying Newsom should push it to 50%, but do it gradually." This is from Newsom's 2025-26 budget proposal (raising the cap to 20%, excluding deposits from the Gann Limit) — and the LAO said he should go further. This strongly supports the "yes" position.

Also, the KPBS article is worth checking to understand the current (October 2026) context. And I could also read the full CBP Center brief, which appears to be in favor. But I think I have enough information. Let me quickly grab the KPBS article to check the current fiscal context and see if there's anything surprising (e.g., an argument that since revenue is currently strong, the state should be saving — supporting "yes"; or an opposing argument that the surplus should be returned).

Actually, let me also quickly confirm that the current state of the state's reserves is as described (the state just spent a lot of its reserve on the 2024-25 and 2025-26 deficits). The LAO's analysis says "currently, the state has about $20 billion in usable reserves for any public program." That's consistent.

I'm confident: **yes**.

Let me quickly grab the KPBS article to confirm the current context, then answer.

California has more revenue than expected thanks to AI. Should the state save it?
By
Yue Stella Yu (https://calmatters.org/author/yue-yu/)
Published October 23, 2026 at 2:39 PM PDT
Facebook (https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.kpbs.org%2Fnews%2Fscience-technology%2F2026%2F10%2F23%2Fcalifornia-has-more-revenue-than-expected-thanks-to-ai-should-the-state-save-it&display=page)
WhatsApp (https://api.whatsapp.com/send?text=California%20has%20more%20revenue%20than%20expected%20thanks%20to%20AI.%20Should%20the%20state%20save%20it%3F%20-%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.kpbs.org%2Fnews%2Fscience-technology%2F2026%2F10%2F23%2Fcalifornia-has-more-revenue-than-expected-thanks-to-ai-should-the-state-save-it)
Email (mailto:?body=California%20has%20more%20revenue%20than%20expected%20thanks%20to%20AI.%20Should%20the%20state%20save%20it%3F%0A%0Ahttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.kpbs.org%2Fnews%2Fscience-technology%2F2026%2F10%2F23%2Fcalifornia-has-more-revenue-than-expected-thanks-to-ai-should-the-state-save-it%0A%0AProponents%20say%20Prop.%202%20would%20allow%20the%20state%20to%20shore%20up%20its%20reserves%20for%20an%20economic%20downturn.%20Critics%20say%20it%20would%20only%20allow%20state%20leaders%20to%20spend%20more%20in%20the%20future.)
Fred Greaves
/
CalMatters
Gov. Gavin Newsom presents his revised 2025-26 budget proposal in Sacramento on May 14, 2025.
This story was originally published by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/) . Sign up (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/) for their newsletters.
The question Proposition 2 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-2-rainy-day-fund/) poses to California voters is simple: Should the state be able to save more money when its economy is booming?
The ballot measure, dubbed the Save for California’s Future Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca20), seeks to shore up California’s rainy day fund by allowing state lawmakers to sock away up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue — double the current ceiling of 10%.
Advertisement
Become a KPBS sponsor (https://www.kpbs.org/corporate-sponsorship)
It would also require the state to save a bigger share of the gains when revenue is growing faster.
Proponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic lawmakers, say the state needs a bigger savings account to weather its volatile economy.
Because California’s tax revenue depends so much on wealthy residents’ stock earnings, the state budget is often caught in a boom-or-bust cycle (https://calmatters.org/explainers/california-budget-whiplash/) at the mercy of the market. In recent years, the state has seen robust tax revenue from an AI-fueled economy, which has helped state leaders avoid or delay painful cuts (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/gavin-newsom-final-budget-plan/) to social services even when they projected significant deficits. But economists have consistently warned the boom may not last, and the federal budget cuts to healthcare and welfare programs this year deepened that uncertainty.
Supporters pitched Prop. 2 as a common sense solution, noting the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, which advises state lawmakers, has long recommended the state set aside funding for downturns. The measure is endorsed by a bipartisan coalition of groups (https://www.yesonprop2.com/#endorsements), including labor unions, hospital associations and chambers of commerce.

California has more revenue than expected thanks to AI. Should the state save it?
By
Yue Stella Yu (https://calmatters.org/author/yue-yu/)
Published October 23, 2026 at 2:39 PM PDT
Facebook (https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.kpbs.org%2Fnews%2Fscience-technology%2F2026%2F10%2F23%2Fcalifornia-has-more-revenue-than-expected-thanks-to-ai-should-the-state-save-it&display=page)

Fred Greaves
/
CalMatters
Gov. Gavin Newsom presents his revised 2025-26 budget proposal in Sacramento on May 14, 2025.
This story was originally published by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/) . Sign up (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/) for their newsletters.
The question Proposition 2 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-2-rainy-day-fund/) poses to California voters is simple: Should the state be able to save more money when its economy is booming?
The ballot measure, dubbed the Save for California’s Future Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca20), seeks to shore up California’s rainy day fund by allowing state lawmakers to sock away up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue — double the current ceiling of 10%.
Advertisement
Become a KPBS sponsor (https://www.kpbs.org/corporate-sponsorship)
It would also require the state to save a bigger share of the gains when revenue is growing faster.
Proponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic lawmakers, say the state needs a bigger savings account to weather its volatile economy.
Because California’s tax revenue depends so much on wealthy residents’ stock earnings, the state budget is often caught in a boom-or-bust cycle (https://calmatters.org/explainers/california-budget-whiplash/) at the mercy of the market. In recent years, the state has seen robust tax revenue from an AI-fueled economy, which has helped state leaders avoid or delay painful cuts (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/gavin-newsom-final-budget-plan/) to social services even when they projected significant deficits. But economists have consistently warned the boom may not last, and the federal budget cuts to healthcare and welfare programs this year deepened that uncertainty.
Supporters pitched Prop. 2 as a common sense solution, noting the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, which advises state lawmakers, has long recommended the state set aside funding for downturns. The measure is endorsed by a bipartisan coalition of groups (https://www.yesonprop2.com/#endorsements), including labor unions, hospital associations and chambers of commerce.
“It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits,” wrote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/10/rainy-day-fund-california-proposition/) Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/jesse-gabriel-160858), an Encino Democrat, and Assembly Appropriations Vice Chair Josh Hoover (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/josh-hoover-165420), a Folsom Republican and the only GOP lawmaker to vote for the measure.
Advertisement
Become a KPBS sponsor (https://www.kpbs.org/corporate-sponsorship)
Most Republican lawmakers opposed Prop. 2, stating that the state should use its excess revenue to give taxpayers refunds instead of saving it. They argue that state government already spends too much and that a bigger reserve would merely give state leaders more to spend.
“When they say we're here for fiscal responsibility, it's like the devil offering a Bible study. Don't buy it,” said (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/279785#t=685&f=074f023444d682ecc1d857e24642a263) Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican.
How long have we had a rainy day fund?
Before 2014, California leaders and voters established reserve funds several times (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) to weather financial storms, but ended up quickly withdrawing most of those funds, leaving the state with very little savings on hand, according to the legislative analyst.
In 2004, following the dot-com bust, voters overwhelmingly supported Prop. 58, a bipartisan ballot measure (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-feb-10-me-dems10-story.htm) that required the state to establish a budget stabilization account and make annual deposits into the fund.
But lawmakers swiftly depleted the fund during the early months of the Great Recession and were forced to make steep spending cuts, borrow money at expensive rates and use accounting gimmicks to weather the rest of the crisis. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees (https://web.archive.org/web/20090809224605/http://www.dpa.ca.gov/news/news/2008/20081106-01.htm) and delayed payments (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2018/3910/recession-recovery-121318.pdf) to schools and local governments.
In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it.
“When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Jerry-Brown-preaches-for-Prop-2-by-talking-up-5812922.php) stumping for the reform.
The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools.
Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years.
A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for.
Bigger reserve = more to spend?
Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending.
“The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.”
“Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.”
In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times.
“I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.”

In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it.
“When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Jerry-Brown-preaches-for-Prop-2-by-talking-up-5812922.php) stumping for the reform.
The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools.
Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years.
A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for.
Bigger reserve = more to spend?
Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending.
“The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.”
“Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.”
In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times.
“I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.”

Now I have a comprehensive overall picture. Let me integrate everything:

**This proposition:** California Proposition 2 (November 2026), "Save for California's Future Act" (ACA 20), a legislative constitutional amendment.

**What it does:**
1. Raises the BSA (rainy day fund) cap from 10% → 20% of General Fund tax revenue.
2. Larger mandatory deposits in years when capital gains tax revenue surges.
3. Extends the mandatory additional debt payments (for pension/retiree health care; expanded to school minimum funding, budget borrowing, and the federal UI loan of about $20 billion) from 2030 → 2040.
4. Gann limit: reserve deposits (BSA + PSHF, up to 10% of GF taxes per year) don't count against the state appropriations limit; withdrawals count against it.

**Arguments in favor / reasons to vote YES:**
- California's revenue is extremely volatile (AI/stock market-driven; a $100 billion surplus in 2022-23, then about a $50 billion deficit in 2024-25/2025-26 due to federal Medi-Cal cuts). LAO: the revenue drop from the 2008-09 recession was about 50% of annual GF tax revenue, and the current 10% cap is "in stark contrast." LAO (nonpartisan) has explicitly recommended a much larger BSA (in 2025, they recommended building up to about 50% of GF taxes over time).
- Current reserves (about $17-20 billion after withdrawals) are insufficient relative to the scale of a typical recession.
- The 2014 Prop. 2 passed with about 70% of the vote; the 2004 Prop. 58 also passed by a wide margin; building the rainy day fund is the established preference of the California electorate.
- The debt payment extension saves interest over the long term (the pension/retiree health care obligations, the UI federal loan).
- SPUR supports it; the California Budget & Policy Center's brief is also favorable; Sacramento Bee and SF Chronicle editorials back it; IGS is neutral.
- Bipartisan: passed 59-8 in the Assembly, 29-2 in the Senate, with the backing of one Republican legislator (Josh Hoover, who co-authored an op-ed with Gabriel).
- Withdrawal guardrails are maintained (budget emergency declaration + legislative vote; withdrawal cap).
- The Gann limit accounting change is roughly neutral in the long run (money counts against the cap when spent, not when saved); under current rules, deposits count against the cap and permanently ratchet up the cap (a known flaw of the Gann limit); under the new rule, savings don't permanently raise the cap.
- Timing: 2026 revenue is high (an AI boom)—it's precisely the good-time window when saving matters; federal funding cuts to Medi-Cal have increased the budget's fragility.

**Arguments against / reasons to vote NO:**
- Tax rebate avoidance (Gann limit). But in 47 years, the rebate mechanism has only been triggered three times: FY87-88 ($1.1 billion), FY2020-21 ($2.8 billion), FY2021-22 ($6 billion—the latter two as pandemic stimulus payments). In 2022-23, no rebate was issued even in a huge surplus. So the "your rebate is being canceled" argument has minimal real-world impact.
- "Slush fund" / politicians will raid it (David Crane's criticism that withdrawal rules allow borrowing against optimistic forecasts). This is a legitimate governance concern, but the same rules apply today, and they're the ones voters approved in 2014.
- The California Policy Center and Reform California (DeMaio) are opposed—mostly from an anti-growth-of-government / pro-spending-cap stance.
- The measure doesn't create any new program funding (a true but narrow point—this is a fiscal stability measure, not a spending bill).

**Verdict:** The weight of independent, nonpartisan fiscal evidence (LAO, SPUR, CBP Center, the historical track record of Prop. 58/Prop. 2 from 2014 with 70% support) supports building a larger rainy day fund. The strongest opposing argument (rebates) is mostly theoretical, given the rebate mechanism's track record and the fact that even in 2022-23's massive surplus, no rebate was issued. The measure also mandates long-term debt reduction that saves money. The risks are manageable, and withdrawal rules are unchanged.

Answer: yes.

I've completed extensive research on this measure — California Proposition 2 (November 2026), the "Save for California's Future Act," a legislative constitutional amendment that would raise the rainy-day fund (Budget Stabilization Account) cap from 10% to 20% of General Fund tax revenue, require larger deposits during revenue booms, extend mandatory debt payments to 2040, and change how reserve deposits count toward the Gann spending limit.

Key findings from my research:

**For a YES vote:**
- The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office has long said the current 10% cap is "stark contrast" to the scale of past recession revenue losses (~50% of General Fund taxes), and in 2025 explicitly said the state should build reserves far beyond 20% (gradually toward ~50%).
- California's revenue is extremely volatile (stock/AI-market dependent): a $100B+ surplus in 2022-23 followed by ~$50B deficits in 2024-25/2025-26, exacerbated by federal Medi-Cal cuts — exactly the boom-bust cycle a larger fund targets.
- Current reserves (~$17-20B after withdrawals) are far below what a typical recession would cost.
- SPUR, the California Budget & Policy Center, Sacramento Bee, and San Francisco Chronicle back it; the 2014 predecessor measure passed with ~70% of the vote.
- Extending mandatory debt repayment through 2040 saves interest on pension/retiree health debts and pays down the ~$20B federal UI loan — long-term money saved.
- The Gann-limit accounting change is economically neutral long-term (money counts when spent, not saved), and actually fixes a flaw where saving permanently ratchets up the spending cap.
- Withdrawal guardrails (budget emergency + legislative vote, capped withdrawals) are unchanged; the Legislature passed it 59-8/29-2, even with a Republican co-sponsor op-ed.

**Against:**
- Main opponent argument is that it makes taxpayer rebates less likely — but the Gann rebate has only been triggered three times in 47 years (1987, and twice as pandemic stimulus), and no rebate was issued even in the 2022-23 mega-surplus, so this is largely theoretical.
- "Slush fund" raiding concerns — real but unchanged from rules voters already approved in 2014.
- Opposition is concentrated in anti-spending-cap groups (Reform California, DeMaio, California Policy Center).

The nonpartisan fiscal consensus, the state's revenue volatility, the recent budget whiplash, and the interest-saving debt provisions all favor expansion of the reserve.

yes

3. Extends the mandatory additional debt payments (for pension/retiree health care; expanded to school minimum funding, budget borrowing, and the federal UI loan of about $20 billion) from 2030 → 2040.
4. Gann limit: reserve deposits (BSA + PSHF, up to 10% of GF taxes per year) don't count against the state appropriations limit; withdrawals count against it.

**Arguments in favor / reasons to vote YES:**
- California's revenue is extremely volatile (AI/stock market-driven; a $100 billion surplus in 2022-23, then about a $50 billion deficit in 2024-25/2025-26 due to federal Medi-Cal cuts). LAO: the revenue drop from the 2008-09 recession was about 50% of annual GF tax revenue, and the current 10% cap is "in stark contrast." LAO (nonpartisan) has explicitly recommended a much larger BSA (in 2025, they recommended building up to about 50% of GF taxes over time).
- Current reserves (about $17-20 billion after withdrawals) are insufficient relative to the scale of a typical recession.
- The 2014 Prop. 2 passed with about 70% of the vote; the 2004 Prop. 58 also passed by a wide margin; building the rainy day fund is the established preference of the California electorate.
- The debt payment extension saves interest over the long term (the pension/retiree health care obligations, the UI federal loan).
- SPUR supports it; the California Budget & Policy Center's brief is also favorable; Sacramento Bee and SF Chronicle editorials back it; IGS is neutral.
- Bipartisan: passed 59-8 in the Assembly, 29-2 in the Senate, with the backing of one Republican legislator (Josh Hoover, who co-authored an op-ed with Gabriel).
- Withdrawal guardrails are maintained (budget emergency declaration + legislative vote; withdrawal cap).
- The Gann limit accounting change is roughly neutral in the long run (money counts against the cap when spent, not when saved); under current rules, deposits count against the cap and permanently ratchet up the cap (a known flaw of the Gann limit); under the new rule, savings don't permanently raise the cap.
- Timing: 2026 revenue is high (an AI boom)—it's precisely the good-time window when saving matters; federal funding cuts to Medi-Cal have increased the budget's fragility.

**Arguments against / reasons to vote NO:**
- Tax rebate avoidance (Gann limit). But in 47 years, the rebate mechanism has only been triggered three times: FY87-88 ($1.1 billion), FY2020-21 ($2.8 billion), FY2021-22 ($6 billion—the latter two as pandemic stimulus payments). In 2022-23, no rebate was issued even in a huge surplus. So the "your rebate is being canceled" argument has minimal real-world impact.
- "Slush fund" / politicians will raid it (David Crane's criticism that withdrawal rules allow borrowing against optimistic forecasts). This is a legitimate governance concern, but the same rules apply today, and they're the ones voters approved in 2014.
- The California Policy Center and Reform California (DeMaio) are opposed—mostly from an anti-growth-of-government / pro-spending-cap stance.
- The measure doesn't create any new program funding (a true but narrow point—this is a fiscal stability measure, not a spending bill).

**Verdict:** The weight of independent, nonpartisan fiscal evidence (LAO, SPUR, CBP Center, the historical track record of Prop. 58/Prop. 2 from 2014 with 70% support) supports building a larger rainy day fund. The strongest opposing argument (rebates) is mostly theoretical, given the rebate mechanism's track record and the fact that even in 2022-23's massive surplus, no rebate was issued. The measure also mandates long-term debt reduction that saves money. The risks are manageable, and withdrawal rules are unchanged.

Answer: yes.

I've completed extensive research on this measure — California Proposition 2 (November 2026), the "Save for California's Future Act," a legislative constitutional amendment that would raise the rainy-day fund (Budget Stabilization Account) cap from 10% to 20% of General Fund tax revenue, require larger deposits during revenue booms, extend mandatory debt payments to 2040, and change how reserve deposits count toward the Gann spending limit.

Key findings from my research:

**For a YES vote:**
- The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office has long said the current 10% cap is "stark contrast" to the scale of past recession revenue losses (~50% of General Fund taxes), and in 2025 explicitly said the state should build reserves far beyond 20% (gradually toward ~50%).
- California's revenue is extremely volatile (stock/AI-market dependent): a $100B+ surplus in 2022-23 followed by ~$50B deficits in 2024-25/2025-26, exacerbated by federal Medi-Cal cuts — exactly the boom-bust cycle a larger fund targets.
- Current reserves (~$17-20B after withdrawals) are far below what a typical recession would cost.
- SPUR, the California Budget & Policy Center, Sacramento Bee, and San Francisco Chronicle back it; the 2014 predecessor measure passed with ~70% of the vote.
- Extending mandatory debt repayment through 2040 saves interest on pension/retiree health debts and pays down the ~$20B federal UI loan — long-term money saved.
- The Gann-limit accounting change is economically neutral long-term (money counts when spent, not saved), and actually fixes a flaw where saving permanently ratchets up the spending cap.
- Withdrawal guardrails (budget emergency + legislative vote, capped withdrawals) are unchanged; the Legislature passed it 59-8/29-2, even with a Republican co-sponsor op-ed.

**Against:**
- Main opponent argument is that it makes taxpayer rebates less likely — but the Gann rebate has only been triggered three times in 47 years (1987, and twice as pandemic stimulus), and no rebate was issued even in the 2022-23 mega-surplus, so this is largely theoretical.
- "Slush fund" raiding concerns — real but unchanged from rules voters already approved in 2014.
- Opposition is concentrated in anti-spending-cap groups (Reform California, DeMaio, California Policy Center).

The nonpartisan fiscal consensus, the state's revenue volatility, the recent budget whiplash, and the interest-saving debt provisions all favor expansion of the reserve.

yes

2
INCREASES STATE’S RAINY DAY FUND. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Increases California's Rainy Day Fund, approved by voters in 2014, to provide funding for education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns. Fiscal Impact : State budget reserves would be higher. Supporters : CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel Opponents : None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.

PRO
Vote yes on Proposition 2 to protect schools, healthcare, and public safety funding. Proposition 2 doubles the state's Rainy Day Fund, stops politicians from overspending when there is a budget surplus, and ensures education funding continues during economic downturns. It has bipartisan support from firefighters, hospitals, health clinics, and educators.
CON
Proposition 2 guarantees more spending, not savings, creating a loophole that makes taxpayer rebates less likely by excluding reserve deposits from California's constitutional spending limit. It provides no new funding for education, healthcare, or public safety. Vote No to protect taxpayer rebates and constitutional limits.
